2.3: Several stumps surrounded the creek landing. Nib climbed the tallest and raised one paw in triumph. From there he could see the reeds, the roof of Reed Hut, and very little of the low pot beside the path. All three invitations still rested in his courier bag.

“Here is lowercase o,” Lark explained clearly. “Its short sound begins on and sits in the middle of pot. Listen: /o/. It is different from the short i in pit. Put p and t around each vowel, and hear how the word changes.”
“Our route key names pot,” Lark invited gently. “Read pot and pit, then choose the marker the note actually names.”

Lark lifted the pot from its low stump. Beneath its base lay a folded crossing note. She read its longer words aloud: the creek handrail needed fastening before the crew crossed. Nib climbed down from his excellent viewing stump. The useful information had been lower than his nose all along. They replaced the pot and walked to the repair shelter.
Dan sat on top. Sam did not.
“Who sat on top in that little passage?” Lark asked gently. “Find the name in the first sentence.”
Lark drew the low pot and its hidden note. Across the creek, Reed Hut waited. The first invitation was still undelivered, but now the crew knew what needed doing before they reached it.
2.4: The repair shelter had two cupboards. Nib chose an enormous empty cap box, imagining how splendid every tool would look inside it. When he lifted it, its corners hid the handrail note. The actual equipment cupboard was small enough to fit beside his bag.

“Lowercase c and lowercase k can both stand for /k/,” Lark modeled clearly. “Hear the short sound in cap, then kit. No extra vowel after it. We'll practice each letter separately before joining it to the sounds we know.”
“Read cap and kit,” Lark encouraged gently. “Which cupboard names the equipment we need?”

Inside the kit cupboard were a short rope and a fastening hook. Lark flew the light rope across to the fixed far post. Nib fastened the near end and checked the line while the walking boards stayed firmly on their supports. They crossed with the compact kit and all three invitations. The giant empty box stayed where it belonged.
Sam can sit on top. Pat can sit on top.
“Can both friends sit on top, or only one?” Lark asked warmly. “Use both sentences.”

Reed Hut's porch was dry under their feet. Behind them the handrail stayed secured. Nib looked down at his small kit with new respect. It had brought exactly enough equipment, with no enormous corners to carry.
2.5: A hat hung over Reed Hut's door handle. Its brim covered the letter flap and most of the caretaker's hanging notice. The caretaker was working in the reeds, so the first delivery needed to follow the instructions left behind. Nib peered beneath the brim as if it might answer him.
“Lowercase h starts hat,” Lark modeled softly. “Let your breath flow gently: /h/. No hum. Join h, a, t into hat. Now change the middle vowel for hot. Hear the difference before you read the notice.”
“Read hat on the hanging notice,” Lark invited gently. “Which thing has been left over the flap?”

Nib moved the hat to its proper hook. The flap appeared below it. He lifted the whole courier bag, then remembered its separate pockets. Lark read the destination on the Reed Hut envelope and posted that invitation alone. The caretaker's note promised a reply in this same flap on the return journey. Two invitations remained packed.
Sam had ham. Pat had hot ham.
“Whose ham was hot?” Lark asked gently. “Find the extra describing word.”

Your journal gained its first completed delivery. Lark marked the flap as the place to collect the reply. Then the crew followed the Mill path, leaving the hat on its hook and the invitation safely inside.
2.6: A shower reached the Mill route shelter before you did. The old visitor pen lay in a wet patch beside a blurred direction page. Nib tried one careful mark. It spread into an impressive puddle of ink. Later couriers would need a clearer direction than that.

“Lowercase e makes the short middle sound in pen,” Lark explained clearly. “Listen to pen and pin. Keep p and n in place while the middle changes. The dry pen can write our message; the pin has a different job.”
“Read pen and pin on the kit pockets,” Lark invited gently. “Find what we need for a readable note.”

Nib held a dry backing beneath a fresh page. Lark used the dry pen to draw the next turn beside a red route post. You could add red beneath the picture using familiar sounds and the new e. They hung the note beneath the roof, where the next shower would miss it. The two remaining invitations stayed dry in their pockets.
Sam met Pat. Pat fed Sam.
“Who fed Sam?” Lark asked gently. “Look at the name that starts the second sentence.”

The wet pen stayed aside to dry. Your working pen returned to the kit. Beyond the shelter, a fallen log lay beside the Mill gate, and the gate would not swing. At least the route to it was clearly recorded now.
2.7: Nib leaned against the fallen log. It did not move. He leaned more grandly. His goggles moved, but the log still did not. The Mill gate caught near its hinge. Lark crouched beside the bottom rail instead of pushing at the largest piece of wood.

“Here g makes the sound at the beginning of gap,” Lark modeled clearly. “Use your voice for the brief /g/, without adding a vowel. Join g, a, p. Other words can give this letter another sound later; today we are using gap and get.”
“Read gap on the repair diagram,” Lark invited softly. “Which small opening does its arrow show beside the hinge?”

Through the gap, Lark could see a loose branch wedged under the hinge. Nib threaded a short strap around that branch. Together they lifted only the loose piece. The heavy log remained stable on the ground. The gate swung free, and your two undelivered invitations entered the Mill yard without a single log being rolled away.
Pat got mad. Sam did not get mad.
“Which friend stayed calm in the little passage?” Lark asked gently. “Read the sentence with not.”

Lark drew the small branch beside the large log. The open gate was the result of moving the right thing. Ahead, round containers crowded the Mill delivery ledge. Nib kept the envelope in his bag while they looked for a flat place.
2.8: The Mill's delivery ledge was full of round tins. Nib balanced an invitation on top. It slid, glided down a curved lid, and landed neatly in his lap. He looked pleased to have caught it and less pleased to have become the delivery shelf.

“Lowercase l begins lip,” Lark explained softly. “Touch your tongue just behind your top teeth and let your voice flow: /l/. Don't add an extra vowel. Join l, i, p. On this diagram, lip means the little raised edge that stops a letter sliding off.”
“Find lip on the shelf sketch,” Lark invited gently. “Which edge could help our envelope stay flat?”

One empty tray covered a lower flat space behind the retaining lip. Nib shifted that tray to an unused support and left the working tins alone. The envelope now had somewhere level to wait. Before posting it, Lark checked the collection diagram. A marked reply box beneath the bench still needed identifying.
Sam let Pat hop. Pat did hop.
“Who did the hopping?” Lark asked gently. “Use the second sentence to check.”

Your journal showed the ledge with its useful lip. The Mill invitation remained retrievable beside the crew, and the Fern Lodge envelope stayed packed. A better shelf was ready; the right box was next.
2.9: Two boxes stood beneath the Mill bench. One was impressively large. The other had an ordinary-sized lid. Nib leaned toward the large box before reading either label. Lark set the invitation on the prepared ledge, where it could wait safely.

“Lowercase b begins bag,” Lark modeled clearly. “A brief voiced /b/, without an extra vowel. Look at b beside d: b has its tall stem first, with the round part on the right. Join b, i, n to read bin.”
“Read bin and kit on these boxes,” Lark invited gently. “Which word names our letter box?”

The correct box was the letter bin, whatever its size. Nib posted the Mill invitation there. Lark read the collection card and drew the same bin on your return-route page. The Mill reply would be left here later. Reed Hut and the Mill now had their invitations. Only Fern Lodge's envelope remained in the courier bag.
“Who hid?” Lark asked softly. “Which sentence gives you that information?”

Lark recorded the second delivery once. Nib closed the empty Mill pocket and lifted the bag. On the next path, a shallow puddle brushed its lower strap. The last invitation was dry, but the bag needed somewhere better to rest.
2.10: The lower strap dipped into muddy water while Nib checked the route book. Fern Lodge's envelope stayed dry inside its protective folio. Nib began to drag the bag away, then stopped when the wet strap pulled against its base. Lark pointed to a low dry stump nearby.

“Lowercase u has the short sound in cup and mud,” Lark modeled clearly. “Listen to cup and cap. The outside sounds stay the same while the middle changes. We've now met five short vowel sounds; we can listen for the one each word actually needs.”
“Read cup and cap in the kit,” Lark invited calmly. “Which one can scoop a little surface water away?”

Nib used the cup beside the strap while Lark brought the bag's handle onto its lifting hook. Together they lifted the bag clear and settled it on the stump without tipping its contents. Nib checked all three pockets. The only remaining invitation was dry. He clipped the muddy cup outside the protected message pocket before setting off again.
Sam dug. Pat sat in mud.
“Who sat in mud?” Lark asked gently. “What did the other friend do?”

Your journal showed the bag lifted clear of the puddle. Beyond the muddy patch, sunlight warmed the Fern Lodge path. A sheltered rest would keep the crew comfortable before the final outward delivery.
2.11: Nib put the umbrella beside a resting board. Its shade fell beautifully over the grass. Unfortunately, the bag was on the board. When Nib moved the bag into the shade, he sat down in the sunny place it had left. Lark watched the patch of light with a thoughtful smile.

“Lowercase w begins wet,” Lark modeled clearly. “Round your lips, then move smoothly into the next sound: /w/. Join w, e, t. Compare wet with the sun label on our resting-place note. The words tell us something about each place.”
“Read wet and sun,” Lark invited gently. “Which place is dry, and what does it still need for a comfortable rest?”

Nib set the bag on the dry board. Lark moved the umbrella's support so its shade covered that board, then anchored its base. Nobody disturbed the spider web beside the shelter. Now the dry resting place was shaded as well. The crew sat together, with Fern Lodge's invitation protected beside them.
Sam got wet. Pat did not get wet.
“Which friend stayed dry?” Lark asked gently. “Find the word that changes what happened.”
After the rest, Fern Lodge's porch was close enough to see. Lark packed the umbrella and checked the route note. A folded receiving sack hung beside the doorway, ready for the last invitation.
2.12: At Fern Lodge, Nib wrapped the final invitation in spare cloth. Then he added another piece, and another, until the destination mark vanished. The caretaker's receiving instructions were fixed beside a folded sack. Lark looked from the neat instruction to the enormous anonymous bundle.

“Here c and k work together for one /k/ sound,” Lark explained clearly. “Read pack, then sack. Don't sound the pair twice. Capital P has the same beginning sound as little p. In Pack it, two words give us one useful instruction.”
“Read Pack it,” Lark invited warmly. “Which protection keeps the envelope safe while leaving its destination visible?”

Nib removed the extra wrapping. The protective folio fitted into the intended sack without hiding the destination. Lark posted the Fern Lodge invitation through the receiving flap. The caretaker's note promised a reply at the same sack hook. All three outward invitations had reached their destinations; the return circuit could begin.
Sam can pack. Pat can pack.
“Can both friends pack?” Lark asked gently. “Check that each sentence tells us so.”

Lark drew the sack hook as your third reply-collection place. Nib's three delivery pockets were empty for a good reason. A small signal bell beside the porch made only a muffled hiss when its cord moved.
2.13: Fern Lodge's reply sack was waiting. Its signal bell was not doing nearly as well. A loose cloth edge lay against the clapper. Nib blew at it with a magnificent puff, and the bell answered with the faintest possible hiss. Lark found the stand's short instruction.

“In bell and fill, the two l letters share one /l/ sound,” Lark explained clearly. “Puff ends with one /f/ written ff. Hiss ends with one /s/ written ss. We still blend the sounds once each; extra letters don't ask for extra little vowels.”
“Read bell on the stand note,” Lark invited gently. “Which part needs room to move?”

Nib lifted the loose cloth and fixed it clear of the clapper. The bell rang once. They collected Fern Lodge's reply from the agreed hook. On the return path they used their own notes: the Mill reply waited in its letter bin, and Reed Hut's reply waited in its flap. Three replies settled into three separate bag pockets.
Sam can fill. Pat can puff.
“Which friend can puff?” Lark asked warmly. “Look at the word after can in each sentence.”

The cloth stayed clear and the bell stayed useful. With every invitation delivered and every reply collected, the crew followed the familiar dry path back to camp. Nothing was still waiting at an unvisited stop.
2.14: At camp, Nib lifted a flag above the new post rack. Lark laid the three replies beneath it. Before they celebrated, each reply needed its destination beside it, and the route book needed the details another courier would actually use. The flag could wait while the record became clear.

“In stamp, keep the beginning sounds close: /s/, /t/,” Lark modeled clearly. “Don't slip a vowel between them. Join the rest, then read step the same way. All the familiar sounds keep their jobs when consonants stand side by side.”
“Read the rack labels and our return notes,” Lark invited warmly. “Which destination belongs with each reply?”

Lark supplied the place names while you checked the short labels and route pictures. Reed Hut's flap, the Mill bin, and Fern Lodge's sack hook matched the three pockets. Nib set the flag above a rack that now told the whole story. Neighbors arrived to use the library, and a little post horn joined your collection.
Sam can stamp. Pat can step.
“Who can stamp?” Lark asked gently. “Which friend has the other job?”

Nib gave the horn one cheerful note. Lark bound fourteen journal chapters into Through the Woods. The post circuit was working: three invitations out, three replies home. One reply invited a later visit to Lookout Hill. Tonight, the second book stood finished beside the first.
